opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's somewhat informative, but you have to be careful about how much you read into it.

Grok 3 reportedly used substantially more training compute than DeepSeek V3, something like an order of magnitude more, depending on whose estimates you trust. Yet on a lot of benchmarks and in people's qualitative experience, Grok 3 was better, but not dramatically better. If you naively assumed capabilities scale smoothly with compute and everyone is equally efficient, you might have expected a bigger gap. So one reading is that the returns to raw pretraining compute are more modest than people thought, or at least that we're at a point on the curve where 10x more compute buys you a meaningful but not transformative improvement.

But I'd push back on putting too much weight on that, for a few reasons.

First, algorithmic efficiency varies a lot between labs. DeepSeek is clearly very good at squeezing performance out of compute: their architecture choices, mixture-of-experts setup, training infrastructure, data work. xAI was a newer lab building fast. So some of what looks like "compute didn't help much" is really "one lab is more compute-efficient than the other." Effective compute, not raw FLOPs, is what matters, and the effective compute gap was probably a lot smaller than the raw gap.

Second, post-training and reasoning RL increasingly matter. A lot of the visible capability now comes from RL on top of the base model, and that's a different axis from pretraining scale. Two models with very different pretraining budgets can end up closer than you'd expect if post-training is the bottleneck on the things people measure.

Third, benchmarks saturate and compress differences. A model that's genuinely somewhat smarter may show only a few points of improvement on benchmarks that are near ceiling or noisy.

So my overall take is that it's a weak update toward "compute alone isn't everything, and efficiency differences between labs are large," which isn't news. I don't think it's strong evidence that scaling is hitting a wall. The cleaner evidence about returns to compute comes from within-lab comparisons, where you're holding the algorithms and data pipeline roughly fixed, and those still look like pretty consistent gains from scaling, plus large gains from RL compute. Cross-lab comparisons like Grok versus DeepSeek have too many confounders to tell you much about the underlying scaling curve.

r001.rationale: It says the gap weakly suggests returns to raw compute may be more modest than people thought, but does not connect that update to what Ryan Greenblatt expected.

r002.rationale: It identifies DeepSeek’s greater compute efficiency and xAI’s newer status as reasons the raw compute gap may overstate the effective compute gap.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that repeating smaller training runs gives DeepSeek more feedback for improving training.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that a first attempt at an order-of-magnitude increase in training scale could introduce execution mistakes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a pretty interesting case to look at. The basic picture is that xAI reportedly used something like an order of magnitude more compute to train Grok 3 than DeepSeek used for V3 and R1 — maybe more than that, depending on how you count — and the result was a model that's somewhat better, but not dramatically better. And I think the naive read of that is, "Oh, compute doesn't matter that much anymore," and I don't think that's quite the right conclusion.

The way I'd think about it is that there are a few different things going on at once. One is that returns to compute have always been roughly logarithmic — you need something like a 10x increase in compute to get a sort of "one step" improvement on whatever the relevant capability is. So a 10x gap producing a modest but real improvement is actually kind of what you'd expect from scaling laws. It's not evidence that scaling broke; it's evidence that scaling is doing what it was always doing, and that one step on a log scale is just less visually dramatic than people sometimes imagine.

The second thing is that compute is not the only input. DeepSeek is, I think, clearly a very strong team with a lot of algorithmic efficiency — things like their mixture-of-experts setup, their attention tricks, their training infrastructure. And xAI was a relatively new lab that was building up its stack quickly. So some of what you're seeing is xAI being somewhat less compute-efficient than DeepSeek, which partially cancels out their raw compute advantage. If you were to compare a frontier lab with mature infrastructure and a 10x compute edge, I'd expect a bigger gap.

And then there's a third thing, which is that a lot of the recent gains have come from post-training — RL on reasoning, that whole cluster — and the amount of compute going into that has been relatively small compared to pretraining. So if the thing that's driving the improvements right now is a part of the pipeline where nobody is yet spending enormous compute, then differences in pretraining compute will show up less in the headline benchmarks. That's a temporary situation, in my view. As labs scale RL compute up, I'd expect compute differences to start mattering more again, not less.

So my overall interpretation is something like: this is mildly evidence toward "algorithmic progress and know-how matter a lot relative to raw compute" — which I already believed — and it's roughly neutral on "does more compute help," because the gap is about what I'd have predicted. What I would take it as evidence against is a view where compute is the only thing that matters and you can just buy your way to the frontier with no catch-up time. That view looks worse after Grok 3.

I'd also just add the caveat that these comparisons are noisy. Benchmarks are partially contaminated, labs cherry-pick which evals to report, and "modest gap" is doing a lot of work in the question — I think reasonable people disagree on how large the gap actually is. So I'd hold all of this somewhat loosely.

r001.rationale: The response calls the gap roughly neutral on whether more compute helps and says it is about what the speaker would have predicted; it does not treat it as evidence of lower returns than expected.

r002.rationale: It says xAI may be less compute-efficient than DeepSeek, partially canceling Grok 3’s raw compute advantage when interpreting the gap.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that repeating smaller training runs gives DeepSeek more feedback for improving training.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that attempting a new order of magnitude of training scale for the first time may cause execution mistakes.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s some evidence that the returns to training compute are relatively modest, but I wouldn’t put that much weight on this particular comparison. You’d really like to compare models trained with the same methods at different compute scales. Here, you’re comparing different teams, potentially using different algorithms and different amounts of inference compute, and we don’t necessarily know the relevant training compute precisely.

If Grok 3 used substantially more training compute and only did a little better, that should update you somewhat against the view that more compute straightforwardly produces huge capability gains. But it’s also consistent with DeepSeek having a more efficient training recipe, such that the extra compute is compensating for an algorithmic disadvantage.

And a modest gap on benchmarks doesn’t necessarily tell you how economically important the difference is. So I’d treat this as a somewhat negative update on the returns to compute, rather than strong evidence that scaling has stopped working.

r001.rationale: The response calls the comparison some evidence that compute returns are modest and a somewhat negative update against expecting huge capability gains.

r002.rationale: It says DeepSeek may have a more efficient training recipe, which could explain the gap independently of training compute.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that repeating smaller runs gives DeepSeek more feedback to improve training.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention execution mistakes from attempting a new order of magnitude of training scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s some evidence that the returns to more training compute are modest, but I’d be pretty cautious about that inference. You’d want to know how much compute actually went into each model, how efficiently it was used, and whether you’re comparing comparable stages of training. Differences in data and training methods could easily obscure the effect you’re trying to measure.

And a small gap on benchmarks doesn’t necessarily mean a small gap in economically useful capabilities. So I’d update somewhat toward larger compute budgets producing less of an advantage, but I wouldn’t treat this comparison as a clean measurement of the scaling curve.

r001.rationale: The response treats the gap as evidence that returns to more compute are modest, but does not say this is lower than Ryan Greenblatt expected.

r002.rationale: It says compute efficiency could confound the comparison, but does not identify Grok as potentially less algorithmically efficient than DeepSeek.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that repeated smaller training runs could give DeepSeek more feedback for improving training.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that a first attempt at an order-of-magnitude increase in scale could lead to execution mistakes.
